hints: Focus on what the peak of a Boltzmann curve actually means, the height shows how many molecules have the most probable energy.
Remember that temperature controls the spread of energies, lower T gives a taller, narrower peak and higher T gives a shorter, flatter peak.
Think about which change makes the curve taller and narrower while keeping the total area the same, and check whether pressure alone changes the shape at constant T.
walkthrough:
**Picture the Boltzmann curve**

Think of the x-axis as molecular energy and the y-axis as number of molecules with that energy. The top of the peak is the most probable energy, so we want that peak to get taller.

The total area under the curve stays constant because the total number of molecules is fixed.

**Recall the effect of temperature**

At low temperature, molecules have similar low energies, so the distribution is narrow and tall. At high temperature, energies spread out, so the distribution is broad and short.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{decrease } T \rightarrow \text{taller, narrower peak}$$
$$\text{increase } T \rightarrow \text{shorter, broader peak}$$

**Recall the effect of pressure at constant temperature**

For an ideal gas, the spread of molecular energies depends only on temperature, not on pressure. Changing pressure at constant T does not change the shape or the peak height.

So keeping T constant while changing P leaves the number at the most probable energy unchanged.

**Apply to the four changes**

We need a taller peak, so we need lower temperature. Keeping pressure constant but decreasing temperature narrows the distribution and raises the peak, giving more molecules with the most probable energy.

options.A: Incorrect. At constant temperature the Boltzmann distribution keeps the same shape. Decreasing pressure does not change the spread of energies, so the peak height stays the same.
options.B: Correct. Decreasing temperature at constant pressure makes fewer molecules have high energy and more cluster around a lower most probable value. The curve becomes narrower and taller, so the number of molecules with the most probable energy increases.
options.C: Incorrect. Like option A, temperature is constant so the energy distribution is unchanged. Increasing pressure does not make the peak taller, it is a common trap to confuse more collisions with a change in energy spread.
options.D: Incorrect. Increasing temperature does the opposite of what is asked. It spreads energies over a wider range, so the curve flattens and the number of molecules with the most probable energy decreases.
